chapter: Biddle, Durham and early road shows
title: Theater pay and being laid off when business turned slow
summary: He earned $25 a week while the manager kept sending the band home on slow days, then laid off the trumpet; Randolph says it taught him to root for the house.

story.theme_name: Getting paid: wages, tips and leaving over money
story.community_name: Getting paid: wages, scale and the pay envelope

blocks.x: Yes. So, we played that for a while. Let me tell you something funny about that theater. Because this entails a lesson that I learned and I -- you see, we would go in the winter and sometimes they'd have those cold days and

the manager of the theater, he'd say -- he'd tell the girls, "Turn the piano on." She'd turn on the electric piano, and they'd tell us, "All right, you all can go home, it's all right." See, we played -- when they didn't have shows, they played the silent pictures anyway, see, played music for silent pictures. All right. But we'd get paid (less (unintelligible)) see.
What was the pay then, do you recall?

Well, it was a very small pay, around about $25.00 -- $25.00 a week. But $25.00 a week at that time and $20.00 a week, and the regular salary was $9.00 a week because men was getting a dollar and a half a day. So, I was kind of half-way rich.

But anyway, now, you watch this twist. The man would send us home three and four times, all right? So, finally after awhile the business began to pick up. I'd look back and when the business picked up, the people were coming in -- oh, I was sitting up thereplaying and I'd be so angry, I would almost want to burst.
Because the people were coming in. Then I couldn't get a chance to go home. See?
So, okay. So, finally, after awhile business began to fall down again, so the man began to send us

home. So, finally, the man says, "Well, as bad as I hate to do this," he says -- and he only had three -- drums, piano and trumpet, he says, "I just have to keep the drums and the piano. I'll have to lay you off -- lay off the trumpet. Randolph, I'll just have to lay you off. I don't know when I can hire you back because the business is just too dull." You know? After that I had pulling for the man. I have really been pulling for the crowd, for the man. Do you follow what I mean?
I learned my lesson. I really learned -- that taught me a lesson.
